sections.h2: What are a McDonough owner's selling choices?
sections.html:
In McDonough you can hand the sale to an agent, run it yourself, or sell to a cash buyer who accepts it in present condition. Each swaps price, time and effort differently.

  • Agent sale: the widest buyer pool, and a closing timeline driven by the buyer's financing.
  • Owner sale: no agent on your side of the deal, so you handle pricing, paperwork and walk-throughs.
  • Cash purchase: fewer contingencies and no repair demands, which helps with inherited houses, tenant problems or payments that have fallen behind.

Whatever you choose, get terms in writing, including who pays the state transfer tax and how property tax is settled at closing.

sections.h2: What do Census tables show for McDonough?
sections.html:
McDonough has grown quickly. The Census Bureau counted 22,084 residents in 2010 and 29,051 in 2020, and it estimates 33,395 for July 1, 2025, which is 14.5% above the April 2020 estimates base of 29,178. The land area is 12.85 square miles, which put 2,260.4 people on each square mile in 2020.

  • Owners occupy 54.8% of homes.
  • A typical owned home is valued at $314,600.
  • Monthly cost of owning with a mortgage: $1,791.
  • Gross rent: $1,792, a little above that mortgage figure.
  • Households: 10,886, averaging 2.76 people.
  • Median household income: $75,343.
  • Residents under 18: 26.4%; age 65 and over: 8.8%.
  • Adults with a bachelor's degree or more: 28.5%.
  • Households with a broadband subscription: 95.6%.
  • Mean commute: 32.5 minutes, longer than the 27.5 minutes listed for Marietta and 28.0 for Milton.

Young residents are a large share: over a quarter are under 18. A seller with a family-sized house can note that the Census lists 2.76 persons per household here, against 2.40 in Marietta.

sections.h2: What local history should a McDonough seller know?
sections.html:
McDonough is the seat of Henry County, about thirty miles southeast of Atlanta. According to the New Georgia Encyclopedia it was incorporated on December 17, 1823, and named for a naval hero of the War of 1812. The town was laid out in blocks with the courthouse originally in the center, near a water source called the Big Spring.

Early businesses served farmers: blacksmith shops, sawmills, grist mills and cotton gins, and the town served as a relay stop on the stagecoach line from New York to New Orleans. By 1921 a hydroelectric plant on the river supplied the city's electricity. Landmarks still standing include the Brown House, begun in 1826, and the Davis-Bryan-Hazlehurst House from around 1829. The city hosts the Geranium Festival in May and the Henry County Fair in the fall. The encyclopedia puts the 2020 census count at 29,051 and says the population rose 160 percent between 2000 and 2010.

Schooling arrived early. Henry County Academy was incorporated in 1824 and began operating in 1827, and the city has a branch of Mercer University within its limits. The McDonough Main Street Program, established in June 2001, works on revitalizing the older business district around the Square through design, economic restructuring, promotion and organization, with an office at 5 Griffin Street.

sections.h2: Which permits and inspections apply inside McDonough?
sections.html:
McDonough's Building and Inspection Division reviews plans and issues permits so that construction meets municipal code. Per the city, work that builds, enlarges, alters, repairs, moves or demolishes a structure needs a permit, as does installing or replacing electrical, gas, mechanical, plumbing or sprinkler systems. Georgia law, O.C.G.A. 43-14, requires licensed trades for plumbing, electrical and heating-air work, and the city states the same applies to homeowners doing that work themselves.

McDonough permit and code contacts from the city's own pages

Permit statusBuilding Division, 770-898-3506

The city enforces the current Georgia State Minimum Codes for Construction as published by the Department of Community Affairs. The list includes the International Residential Code, the International Energy Conservation Code, the National Electrical Code and the International Property Maintenance Code. Water and sewer tap applications and an irrigation meter application are on the same division's forms page, and an Owner Occupied Housing Rehabilitation Program application is listed there too.

Code Compliance sits inside the Planning and Zoning Division of Community Development. The city notes that the Mayor and Council adopt the codes but do not handle individual compliance cases. Code Compliance officers usually notify the person responsible, explain how to fix the violation and allow a set time. If voluntary efforts fail, a citation sends the matter to McDonough Municipal Court.

The Building Division's forms page separates residential from commercial permit applications and posts a permit fee schedule, so pull the residential form and fee list if you are unsure what an earlier repair required.

Before listing, check that decks, water heaters, additions or finished basements were permitted. The city says work done without the proper permits can be penalized, and a buyer's inspector may ask for proof.

sections.h2: How do Henry County assessments and appeals affect a McDonough sale?
sections.html:
Henry County's Tax Assessor pages cover the Notice of Assessment, Property Appeals, Homestead Exemption, Conservation Use and Property Returns. Georgia's appeal statute, O.C.G.A. 48-5-311, is the state framework, and the Macon-Bibb assessors' summary of it explains that the written appeal is due 45 days after the notice date. A McDonough owner follows the same statewide process, so go by the date printed on your own notice.

Because the notice shows the assessed value and an estimate of taxes, it is worth keeping with your sale papers. Before choosing a closing date, request your current bill, due dates and balance from the Henry County Tax Commissioner, and ask the Tax Assessor which exemptions your house carries. A homestead exemption belongs to the seller and ends at the sale, so the buyer files a new application for their own exemption after closing.

sections.h2: What is the transfer tax on a McDonough sale?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded by the Henry County Clerk of Superior Court after the state tax is paid. That tax is $1 for the first $1,000 of price or any fraction thereof, plus 10 cents per additional $100 or fraction thereof.

The seller is liable under O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10, although many sales contracts make the buyer pay. The PT-61 form is filled out online with the state clerks' cooperative, and a printed copy goes to the clerk with the deed. Exemption questions belong with the Henry County clerk.

faqs.q: Is an open McDonough code violation a barrier to selling?
faqs.a: Yes, though the cleanest path is to resolve it first. McDonough's Code Compliance Division normally gives the responsible person time to fix a violation and cites them to Municipal Court if that fails. Report or ask about a case through the hotline at 470-878-1150.

faqs.q: How soon can I get a building inspection in McDonough?
faqs.a: Call the inspection request line at 678-782-6217 before 4 p.m. for a next-day inspection. Requests after 4 p.m. are scheduled two days out, and Friday or holiday calls before 4 p.m. go to the next working day.

faqs.q: What is a typical home worth in McDonough?
faqs.a: The Census figure for 2020 to 2024 is $314,600 for an owned home, with 54.8% of homes owner-occupied. Your own house will price by its condition and location.

faqs.q: Who owes transfer tax in a McDonough sale?
faqs.a: The statute puts it on the seller, and many contracts shift it. Read yours, and ask the Henry County clerk if an exemption might apply.

faqs.q: What should I ask Henry County before closing on my McDonough house?
faqs.a: Get the current bill and any balance from the Tax Commissioner, and the exemption list from the Tax Assessor. Also confirm your house sits inside McDonough city limits, since the city's permit and code rules apply only there.
